article.title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
article.subtitle: All the numbers for Trump vs. Harris.

extraction.summary: This is the final landing page of the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast, run at midnight on Election Day. Out of 80,000 simulations, Harris won 50.015%, Trump 49.648% outright, and 270 simulations (about 0.34%) were 269-269 ties. The text says the model is a direct descendant of the Silver-era FiveThirtyEight model, with methodology largely unchanged except that the 2020 COVID provisions were removed. It summarizes the polling-average mechanics: registered/likely voter adjustment, house effects, reliability weighting, and national-state inference. The embedded charts reveal the most model detail: the step-by-step pipeline from polling average to win probability with blend weights, the six-indicator economic index, the Electoral College bias by popular-vote margin, scenario shifts, tipping-point and Voter Power Index definitions, and conditional state probabilities that show strong correlation between states. The post is marked paywalled, but the forecast content appears fully present.

findings.statement: The final run of the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model used 80,000 simulations. Harris won 40,012 (50.015%), Trump won 39,718 outright, and 270 were exact 269-269 Electoral College ties.
findings.evidence_quote: Out of 80,000 simulations, Kamala Harris won in 40,012 (50.015%) cases.

findings.statement: The chart captions on the 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast page describe results as based on 40,000 simulations, while the text says the final run used 80,000. The standard per-update simulation count may therefore be 40,000, with the final run doubled, or the chart captions may simply be stale.

findings.statement: The 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model counts exact 269-269 ties as a separate 'no majority' outcome rather than as a win for either candidate. The authors note these ties would likely resolve as Trump wins in the House contingent election.
findings.rationale: Republicans were expected to control more House state delegations.
findings.evidence_quote: these ties are likely to eventually result in Trump wins in the U.S. House of Representatives

findings.statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model, the 'no majority' outcome can also arise if a third-party candidate receives electoral votes, not only from 269-269 ties.

The 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model forecasts Maine and Nebraska congressional districts (ME-1, ME-2, NE-2, NE-3) as separate contests, because those states award one electoral vote per district plus two to the statewide winner.

The 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model is a direct descendant of the FiveThirtyEight forecast Silver built, with largely the same methodology. The main change from 2020 is the removal of the COVID-19 provisions introduced for that cycle; other changes are documented in a separate post. Silver retained the intellectual property rights to the model.
findings.evidence_quote: the methodology is largely the same, other than removing COVID-19 provisions introduced for 2020

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages adjust polls according to whether they were conducted among registered or likely voters. Poll populations are labeled LV (likely voters), RV (registered voters), V (voters) and A (adults).
findings.evidence_quote: They adjust for whether polls are conducted among registered or likely voters

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages adjust for each pollster's house effect.

The Silver Bulletin polling averages weight more reliable pollsters more heavily. Each poll's weight reflects its quality, sample size and recency, and each poll's 'influence' on the average is displayed.
findings.evidence_quote: They weight more reliable polls more heavily.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages use national polls to make inferences about state polls and vice versa. State averages are adjusted based on trends in both state and national polls.
findings.rationale: The extra computation yields a more stable average that is not thrown off by outliers.
findings.evidence_quote: they use national polls to make inferences about state polls and vice versa

findings.statement: Silver favors a computationally heavier polling average because stability and robustness to outliers are worth the extra cost.
findings.evidence_quote: the reward is a more stable average that doesn’t get psyched out by outliers

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling-average table only displays contests surveyed by at least three distinct pollsters or with at least five polls. Week and month changes compare against the averages 7 and 30 days before the latest update.

The 2024 Silver Bulletin model converts a state polling average into a forecast in 10 steps. These are: (1) polling average; (2) adjust for bounces and recent events; (3) adjusted polling average; (4) reallocate undecideds and third-party votes; (5) reallocated vote share; (6) blend with a regression; (7) snapshot; (8) blend with economic fundamentals; (9) projected vote share; (10) chance of winning.
The 2024 Silver Bulletin model includes a step that adjusts state polling averages for bounces and recent events, such as conventions. By Election Day this adjustment was ±0.0 in Arizona.

In the 2024 Silver Bulletin model, undecided and third-party vote is reallocated to the major candidates. In the final Arizona forecast, Harris and Trump each received +1.4 points, an equal split, taking them from 46.9/49.3 to 48.3/50.7.

In the 2024 Silver Bulletin model, the polling average is blended with a state-level regression estimate. On Election Day the regression weight in Arizona was 0.01; the regression estimate was 48.2/50.8, against 48.3/50.7 from polls.

In the 2024 Silver Bulletin model, the polls-based 'snapshot' is blended with economic fundamentals. On Election Day the fundamentals weight was 0.00, so the projected vote share equaled the snapshot. The fundamentals estimate in Arizona was 47.4/51.6, more favorable to Trump than the polls.
The 2024 Silver Bulletin model places less weight on fundamentals as Election Day approaches, reaching roughly zero on Election Day.

The Silver Bulletin Economic Index (SBEI) averages z-scores of six indicators: real disposable personal income, consumer price index, nonfarm payrolls, industrial production, personal consumption expenditures, and the S&P 500. Variables are standardized to roughly the same mean and standard deviation; zero is an average economy. Readings cover the two years before the election, with heavier weight on recent data, and are projected forward to Election Day.

Final 2024 SBEI z-scores were: RDPI −0.21, CPI +0.48, nonfarm payrolls +0.07, industrial production −0.43, PCE +0.24, S&P 500 +0.91, for an average of +0.18. That means a slightly above-average economy.

The scenario table in the 2024 Silver Bulletin model shifts all polls toward one candidate by 1-5 points, adjusting for each state's elasticity, while fundamentals continue to influence the result. Each 1-point shift moves win probability by roughly 10-11 points near a tied race; Harris +1 gives 61.0% and Trump +1 gives 60.9%.

In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin simulations, the Electoral College favored Trump: Harris won only 14.3% when winning the popular vote by 0-1, 32.5% at D+1-2 and 58.2% at D+2-3. Trump won 94.0% at R+0-1.

Final 2024 Silver Bulletin topline: Harris Electoral College probability 50.0%, Trump 49.6%, no majority 0.3%. Popular-vote probability was Harris 76.2% and Trump 23.8%. Predicted electoral votes were 271.0 to 267.0, and predicted popular vote 50.5% to 48.4%.

The final 2024 Silver Bulletin projected national margin (Harris 50.5 to 48.4, about D+2.1) is larger than the national polling average (48.6 to 47.6, D+1). This suggests that undecided/third-party reallocation and other pipeline steps change the margin, not just the levels.

States are strongly correlated in the 2024 Silver Bulletin simulations. Trump winning all seven battlegrounds was the single most likely scenario at 20.0%, and Harris winning all seven was next at 13.9%. Winning Pennsylvania gave Harris a 90.4% and Trump an 87.9% chance of winning overall.

findings.statement: A contest's 'chance of tipping the election' in the 2024 Silver Bulletin model is the probability that it gives the Electoral College winner their 270th electoral vote. The Voter Power Index (VPI) is the relative likelihood that an individual voter in that state determines the Electoral College winner.

The '128 paths' table in the 2024 Silver Bulletin model enumerates all 2^7 win/loss combinations of the seven likeliest tipping-point states. Every other state is assigned to its forecast leader, and the table shows each scenario's probability and Harris's EC win probability. For example, R in AZ, GA, NC and NV with D in MI, PA and WI gives exactly 270 EVs and an 82.5% Harris win probability.
The 2024 Silver Bulletin model reports a forecast margin for each contest with 10th-90th percentile intervals, so 80% of outcomes fall within the interval shown.

The 2024 Silver Bulletin model defines a 'recount' scenario as one or more decisive states within 0.5 percentage points and gave it an 11% chance. Other final scenario probabilities: Harris wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College 26%; Trump wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College 0%; Harris majority 63%; Trump majority 14%; Harris landslide 1%.

findings.statement: In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast, Pennsylvania (R+0.1) was the tipping-point state on the ordered path. Harris led Wisconsin by D+1 and Michigan by D+1.2, while Trump led Nevada R+0.5, Georgia R+1, North Carolina R+1.1 and Arizona R+2.4.

The Electoral College distribution in the 2024 Silver Bulletin simulations is lumpy and multimodal. The most frequent Harris outcome was 226 EVs (about 6%, the all-battlegrounds-to-Trump map), with a second peak near 319 (about 3%).

The 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast launched with Trump at about 62% against Harris at about 37%. Harris led through August; Trump peaked near 64% around September 8, just before the debate; Harris peaked near 58% in late September; the race converged to about 50-50 by November 5.

The Silver Bulletin national polling average and forecast tracked Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as a third candidate until he dropped out in late August 2024. His average fell from about 15% in June to about 4%.

Silver presents forecasts as probabilistic best guesses, not predictions. He stresses that trailing candidates win often enough, that in a polarized era most elections are close, and that he reports probabilities even to the decimal place.
findings.evidence_quote: stranger things have happened than a candidate who was behind in the polls winning

findings.statement: The 2024 Silver Bulletin model publishes raw output files that are updated with each forecast run. They are: Econ Index, EV Probabilities, Election Paths, EC vs Popvote, Scenario Analysis, Forecast Steps, National Topline, Pres Pollist, Voteshare Probabilities, Poll Average and State Topline.
findings.evidence_quote: These spreadsheets contain the raw output from our forecast model.

political_insights.insight: In 2024 the Electoral College was expected to favor Republicans by roughly 2-3 points. Harris needed about a D+2.5 popular-vote margin to be a slight favorite.
political_insights.evidence: Harris won 14.3% of simulations at D+0-1, 32.5% at D+1-2 and 58.2% at D+2-3. Harris winning the popular vote but losing the Electoral College had a 26% chance.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model state outcomes relative to the national vote rather than assuming the popular-vote winner takes the Electoral College.

political_insights.insight: A 269-269 tie would likely be decided for Trump in the House, which votes by state delegation.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Allocate tie outcomes to the party with more House state delegations when computing effective win probability.

political_insights.insight: In a polarized climate, most presidential elections are close and candidates are rarely out of the running.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Avoid overconfidence; keep meaningful tail probabilities.

political_insights.insight: The seven 2024 swing states tend to move together, so sweeps by either side are the likeliest outcomes.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Use strongly correlated state errors in simulation.

open_questions: Why the final run used 80,000 simulations when charts cite 40,000; what the standard per-update count is.
What the COVID-19 provisions from 2020 were, which were removed.
The functional form and schedule by which regression and fundamentals weights decline toward zero over the campaign.
How undecided and third-party vote is reallocated (equal split versus proportional) and under what conditions.
Which variables are in the state-level regression blended with the polls.
How the SBEI translates into a vote-share forecast and what decay weights apply over the two-year window.
How state 'elasticity' is estimated for the scenario shifts.
The size and distribution of the polling error, fat tails, and the state correlation structure.
How the bounce and recent-events adjustment is parameterized, for conventions and debates.
How likely voter/registered voter and house-effect adjustments are computed, and the exact pollster weight formula.
